title: How do you achieve deep cloning of an object (serialization, copy constructor, JSON round-trip)?
shortTitle: How do you achieve deep cloning?

s1_definition.profdef: Deep cloning produces a copy of an object in which every mutable object it references is also copied recursively, so the original and the clone share no mutable state. The three practical techniques are a manual copy constructor or copy factory that explicitly rebuilds each mutable field, a serialization round-trip that writes the object graph to bytes and reads it back, and a JSON round-trip using a library like Jackson that serializes to JSON and deserializes into a new object. Each technique guarantees independence but differs in speed, required library support, and how it handles cycles and transient fields.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh's account file at National Bank of India has a cover page and a stapled booklet of past statements, and each statement has its own attached receipts. A deep clone means that when you copy the file, you also re-create the booklet and re-create every receipt, so the copy is a fully independent file. The three ways to do this are: a clerk who carefully re-types every page by hand into a fresh file (copy constructor), a machine that scans the whole file to microfilm and prints a brand new file from it (serialization), or converting the whole file to a plain-text description and then building a fresh file from that description (JSON round-trip).
s1_definition.oneliner: Deep cloning copies the whole object graph so nothing mutable is shared, and the three common ways are a copy constructor, a serialization round-trip, and a JSON round-trip.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Deep cloning produces a copy of an object in which every mutable object it references is also copied recursively, so the original and the clone share no mutable state. The three practical techniques are a manual copy constructor or copy factory that explicitly rebuilds each mutable field, a serialization round-trip that writes the object graph to bytes and reads it back, and a JSON round-trip using a library like Jackson that serializes to JSON and deserializes into a new object. Each technique guarantees independence but differs in speed, required library support, and how it handles cycles and transient fields.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh's account file at National Bank of India has a cover page and a stapled booklet of past statements, and each statement has its own attached receipts. A deep clone means that when you copy the file, you also re-create the booklet and re-create every receipt, so the copy is a fully independent file. The three ways to do this are: a clerk who carefully re-types every page by hand into a fresh file (copy constructor), a machine that scans the whole file to microfilm and prints a brand new file from it (serialization), or converting the whole file to a plain-text description and then building a fresh file from that description (JSON round-trip).

**One line to remember:** Deep cloning copies the whole object graph so nothing mutable is shared, and the three common ways are a copy constructor, a serialization round-trip, and a JSON round-trip.

sections.s2_technical:
The first and most recommended technique is a copy constructor or copy factory. You write a constructor that takes an existing object and rebuilds each field, deep-copying mutable sub-objects and sharing immutable ones. For a nested structure you call the nested type's copy constructor too, cascading the deep copy down the graph. For example, `new Portfolio(existing)` where the portfolio constructor does `this.holdings = existing.holdings.stream().map(Holding::new).collect(toList());` to copy each holding. The advantage is full control, compile-time safety, no reflection, and the best performance. The disadvantage is you must write and maintain the code, and you must remember to deep-copy every mutable field.

The second technique is a serialization round-trip. You write the object to an ObjectOutputStream backed by a byte array, then read it back from an ObjectInputStream. Deserialization constructs an entirely new graph, so it is deep by construction, and it even handles shared references and cycles correctly because the stream tracks object identity. The code is essentially the `deepCopy` helper: serialize to a byte array, then deserialize. Apache Commons `SerializationUtils.clone(obj)` wraps this. The requirements are that every class in the graph implements Serializable, and transient fields are not copied, which can be either a feature or a surprise. It is slower than a copy constructor because it does real input and output work and reflection.

The third technique is a JSON round-trip, typically with Jackson: `String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(obj); Portfolio copy = mapper.readValue(json, Portfolio.class);`. This produces a deep copy because Jackson builds a new object tree from the JSON text. It does not require Serializable, only that the class is serializable to JSON, meaning it has accessible fields or getters and a way to construct it. The trade-offs are that it loses type information for polymorphic fields unless you configure type handling, it does not preserve object identity so two references to the same sub-object become two separate copies, and numbers can lose precision, which is dangerous for money unless you keep BigDecimal fields and configure Jackson to preserve them.

The senior-level guidance is to default to a copy constructor for domain objects you control, because it is explicit, fast, and type-safe, and to reach for serialization or JSON only when the graph is large, deeply nested, or you do not control all the classes. A crucial money-handling caution is to verify that whichever technique you choose preserves BigDecimal precision and never silently converts to a floating-point type. Another nuance is cyclic references: the serialization approach handles cycles, a naive copy constructor can infinite-loop on them, and JSON round-trips typically fail on cycles unless configured.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India models Rajesh's investment portfolio as a portfolio object that contains a list of holdings, and each holding has its own mutable details. Before the bank runs a what-if rebalancing simulation, it must clone the whole portfolio deeply so the simulation cannot touch the real portfolio. This is exactly what deep cloning solves, because only a fully independent copy keeps the simulation safe.

Problem 2 — The team needs three ways to do this depending on context: a fast copy constructor for the normal path, a serialization round-trip for a quick generic deep copy, and a JSON round-trip for exporting to an external analytics tool and reconstructing. This is exactly why we implement all three techniques and compare them.

In the mini-project we build a `Portfolio` containing a list of `Holding` objects. We deep-clone it three ways: a cascading copy constructor, a serialization round-trip, and a JSON round-trip using a tiny hand-rolled serializer to stay dependency-free in the demo. The main method mutates the original and proves all three clones are unaffected.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Portfolio named Rajesh-PF holding RELIANCE (100 shares at 2450.50) and TCS (50 shares at 3600.00). Three deep clones are taken, then the original's first holding is changed.

Step 1: The original portfolio is built with its own ArrayList and two Holding objects.

Step 2: The copy constructor runs. It makes a new ArrayList and, for each original holding, calls the Holding copy constructor, so every holding is a fresh object. The clone shares nothing mutable.

Step 3: The serialization round-trip writes the whole graph to a byte array and reads it back. Deserialization builds a brand new portfolio and brand new holdings, so it is deep.

Step 4: The text round-trip encodes the portfolio into a delimited string, then parses that string back into fresh Holding objects and a fresh portfolio, which is also deep.

Step 5: The original's first holding quantity is set to 999 and its price to 9999.99. Because all three clones are independent, their first holding still shows quantity 100, proving the deep copies worked.

```text
[INFO] ORIGINAL first holding qty=999
[INFO] copy(ctor)   first holding qty=100
[INFO] copy(serial) first holding qty=100
[INFO] copy(text)   first holding qty=100
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Deep cloning means producing a copy of an object in which every mutable object it references is also copied recursively, so the original and the clone share no mutable state at all. There are three practical techniques I use, and I choose between them based on the situation. The first and my default is a copy constructor or copy factory, where I write a constructor that takes an existing object and rebuilds each field, deep-copying the mutable sub-objects and sharing the immutable ones. When the object contains nested objects, I cascade the deep copy by calling each nested type's own copy constructor, so the copy flows all the way down the graph. In my portfolio example, the portfolio copy constructor builds a new list and re-creates each holding with the holding copy constructor. This approach is the fastest, it is type-safe, it needs no reflection, and the copy depth is explicit in the code.

The second technique is a serialization round-trip, where I write the object to an ObjectOutputStream backed by a byte array and then read it back from an ObjectInputStream. Deserialization constructs an entirely new graph, so it is deep by construction, and it even handles shared references and cycles correctly because the stream tracks object identity. Apache Commons wraps this as SerializationUtils dot clone. The requirements are that every class in the graph implements Serializable and that I remember transient fields are not copied. It is slower than a copy constructor because it does real input and output and uses reflection, so I use it when the graph is large or I do not want to hand-write the copy logic.

The third technique is a JSON round-trip, typically with Jackson, where I serialize the object to a JSON string and deserialize it into a brand new object. This produces a deep copy and does not require Serializable, only that the type is expressible as JSON. The trade-offs I am careful about are that a JSON round-trip loses object identity so two references to the same sub-object become two separate copies, it can lose polymorphic type information unless I configure type handling, and it can lose numeric precision.

The senior point I always stress, because this is banking, is money precision. Whichever technique I choose, I verify it preserves BigDecimal and never silently drops to a floating-point type, since a rounding error in a clone could flow back into a real position. I also keep cycles in mind: serialization handles them, a naive copy constructor can infinite-loop on them, and a JSON round-trip usually fails on them. So my rule is: copy constructor by default for domain objects I control, serialization for large graphs I do not want to hand-copy, and JSON only when I am already crossing a service or tool boundary.

---

keyPoints: Override clone() and manually clone each mutable field
Copy constructor: new Account(original) — clone each nested object
Serialization trick: serialize then deserialize — creates fully independent copy
Always test: modify the clone and verify original is unaffected
